full_query:
A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain. He first felt the pain while lifting boxes at work but thought that he had just strained a muscle. The pain appears to be worse in the mornings and after rest. Exercise and physical activity appear to temporarily make the pain better. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen for the pain. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is found to have limited flexion and extension of his spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of his patellar tendons bilaterally. Results from laboratory tests are shown below:

Serum:
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 61 mm/hr
C-reactive protein (CRP): 36 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L)

Which of the following is the most accurate test for this patient's condition? (A) Bone scan (B) Computed tomography (C) Magnetic resonance imaging (D) Radiograph (E) Ultrasound

shared_context.chief_complaint: 6-month history of increasing lower back pain
shared_context.exam_findings: limited flexion and extension of spine; bilateral tenderness over patellar tendon insertions (enthesitis)

sentences: To determine the most accurate test for the condition described in the question, we need to consider the patient's symptoms, physical examination findings, and laboratory test results in the context of common clinical scenarios
A 26-year-old man with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain
Pain worsens in the mornings and after rest, which suggests inflammatory back pain
Pain improves with exercise and physical activity
Limited flexion and extension of the spine
Tenderness over the insertion of the patellar tendons bilaterally (enthesitis)
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 61 mm/hr
The combination of chronic back pain, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, and enthesitis suggests a spondyloarthropathy, such as ankylosing spondylitis (AS)
Bone Scan: Not typically used for the initial diagnosis of spondyloarthropathies
Computed Tomography (CT): Useful for detecting bony changes but less sensitive than MRI for early inflammatory changes
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Highly sensitive for detecting early inflammatory changes and sacroiliitis, which are characteristic of AS
Radiograph: Useful for detecting advanced bony changes like syndesmophytes but less sensitive for early disease
Ultrasound: Useful for detecting enthesitis but not typically used for diagnosing axial involvement
Given the clinical suspicion of ankylosing spondylitis and the need to detect early inflammatory changes, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the most accurate test for this patient's condition
MRI can reveal early signs of sacroiliitis and other inflammatory changes in the spine and sacroiliac joints that are characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis
